claims.text: Atomic layer deposition can form an ultrathin, precisely controlled TiO2 shell around preformed Pt nanoparticles on γ-Al2O3.
The TiO2 shell acts as a physical barrier that inhibits Pt nanoparticle sintering.
An ultrathin TiO2 shell permits reactants to access the Pt catalyst.
The TiO2 shell facilitates electron transfer involving the Pt core.
The TiO2 shell protects Pt nanoparticles from agglomeration during high-temperature redox cycling.
Suppressing Pt agglomeration preserves the catalyst's active Pt surface area.
Preservation of active Pt surface area enhances catalytic reaction kinetics.
Maintaining Pt dispersion improves catalyst durability under harsh thermal and chemical conditions.
A TiO2-coated catalyst can retain high activity and durability while using less Pt than an uncoated Pt/γ-Al2O3 catalyst.
Optimized TiO2-coated catalysts will provide CO and hydrocarbon conversion comparable to or better than uncoated Pt/γ-Al2O3 despite lower Pt content.
Optimized TiO2-coated catalysts will show improved stability during extended thermal aging.
The beneficial effects of the TiO2 shell will persist during cycling from 600 to 800 °C under alternating rich and lean conditions.
A TiO2 shell that is too thick will impede reactant diffusion and may eliminate the performance benefit.
A TiO2 shell that is too thin will fail to prevent Pt sintering and may eliminate the performance benefit.
